items.title: [ScienceDaily] Astronauts’ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars
items.content_html: A new study tracking 13 astronauts suggests that the human heart may be surprisingly well equipped for a journey to Mars, especially with regular exercise during spaceflight. Researchers found that astronauts' hearts adapted to months of weightlessness and handled simulated Martian gravity without major problems, offering new hope for future missions to the Red Planet.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Rejuvenation breakthrough: Scientists reverse 60 years of aging in human cells
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Scientists have turned blood cells from an 80-year-old into neural stem cells with a molecular age of less than 20, effectively reversing more than 60 years of cellular aging in the laboratory. The discovery offers a new way to investigate how cells become younger and could help researchers better understand age-related diseases such as Alzheimer's.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
items.content_html: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists finally uncover why statins can cause muscle pain
items.content_html:
🎨 🏔️ ✏️

Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why statins, the widely prescribed cholesterol-lowering drugs that help prevent heart attacks and strokes, can sometimes cause muscle pain, weakness, and even severe muscle damage. Using advanced imaging technology, researchers discovered that statins can attach to a crucial protein in muscle cells and force open a channel that normally controls calcium flow. This causes calcium to leak continuously, potentially damaging muscle tissue.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimer’s-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. The strongest benefits appeared at 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps, suggesting that the popular 10,000-step goal may not be necessary.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A simple touch can bring dying corals back to life in just 7 weeks
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🪶 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Scientists have discovered that severely bleached corals can make a remarkable comeback simply by touching healthy, genetically identical corals. In laboratory experiments, dying corals regained their color and fully recovered within seven weeks, with as little as five days of contact sometimes enough to start the healing process.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize for controlling brain cells with light
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

A discovery in tiny algae led to a Nobel Prize-winning breakthrough that allows scientists to switch brain cells on and off using light. The revolutionary technique has already helped researchers activate memories and is opening new possibilities for restoring vision and treating brain disorders.

items.content_html:

Scientists have uncovered an unexpected culprit behind sleep loss in Alzheimer’s disease: overactive immune cells in the brain. By temporarily removing these cells, researchers restored more than two hours of sleep per day in mice, revealing a promising new target for treatment.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Physicists create a bizarre new quantum state called a fractional fermi sea
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Physicists have discovered a strange new state of quantum matter in which ultracold atoms defy familiar organizational rules, forming a highly excited yet surprisingly orderly configuration called a "fractional Fermi sea." The discovery challenges established quantum theories and hints at exotic quasiparticles that scientists have dubbed potential "super-Fermions."

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover that male and female skin play by different rules
items.content_html:
🔧 🔭 ✏️

Scientists have uncovered a surprising difference in how male and female skin repairs and renews itself. By tracking individual skin stem cells in living mice for five months, researchers discovered that female cells work together in a highly coordinated way, while male cells operate more independently. This synchronization, driven by sex hormones, helps explain why wounds heal faster in female mice, especially during the first few days.

items.content_html: Scientists have discovered that many common sweeteners can interfere with gut bacteria, with some combinations involving medications producing surprisingly strong effects. One sweetener mixed with a widely prescribed antidepressant reduced beneficial bacteria and microbial diversity in laboratory experiments, raising new questions about potential effects on gut health and immunity.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease by repairing the gut
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered that a potential new drug can reverse severe fatty liver disease in animal models by restoring gut health and blocking harmful substances from reaching the liver. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments for liver disease and potentially other serious conditions, including cardiovascular disease.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
items.content_html: Scientists have uncovered a surprising cause of age-related cognitive decline involving brain cells previously thought to be entirely beneficial. As these cells become dysfunctional, they can produce abnormal amounts of myelin, disrupting nerve fibers and potentially contributing to worsening memory and thinking skills.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Scientists have discovered that some forest soils are becoming surprisingly better at removing methane from the atmosphere as temperatures rise and rainfall declines. A study spanning up to 24 years found methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% annually, challenging previous predictions about climate change's effects on forests.
